subject: History
source: Edexcel GCSE History 1HI0 Paper 1: Crime and punishment in Britain, c1000-present (option 11) with Whitechapel, c1870-c1900 as the paired historic environment; Papers 2 and 3 options chosen for the school: Superpower relations and the Cold War 1941-91 with Early Elizabethan England 1558-88, and Weimar and Nazi Germany 1918-39 (Y11 file). Phase 1 covers Key Topic 1 (c1000-c1500). No school Drive history material for this option, written from the specification and subject knowledge

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Crime and punishment in medieval England, c1000-c1500
lessons.title: Crime, law and punishment: the big picture and Anglo-Saxon crime
objectives: Define crime, law enforcement and punishment, and explain the factors that cause change over time
Describe the types of crime and the aims of law in Anglo-Saxon England c1000

keywords.def: an act that breaks the law of the time and place
when things stay the same over time
when things become different over time
the idea that the king was responsible for keeping order and safety
something that causes change or continuity, such as religion, government or attitudes

starter: Give one example of something that is a crime today but was not a crime 100 years ago, or the reverse.
Who made the laws in England around the year 1000?

teach.heading: Bismillah: why study crime over 1,000 years?
bullets: Thematic study: c1000 to the present
We track continuity and change over time
Justice and fairness are central values
teach.note: Begin with bismillah and link to the Islamic emphasis on justice (adl): the Qur'an commands justice, e.g. 4:135 and 5:8. Explain that this course covers about 1,000 years in four key topics, so we must think about patterns not just events.

teach.heading: Factors that cause change
bullets: Religion and the Church
Government and the state
Attitudes and social change
War, poverty and new technology
teach.note: Introduce the Edexcel thematic approach: factors such as the Church, central government, attitudes, individuals and science. Ask pupils to give one factor that might change a punishment. Revisit these factors in every lesson.

teach.heading: Anglo-Saxon crime c1000
bullets: Crimes against the person: murder, assault
Crimes against property: theft, arson
Crimes against authority: treason, disobeying the king
teach.note: Emphasise the three categories used throughout the course. Ask pupils which type of crime was seen as most serious and why. Treason against the lord or king was the worst.

teach.heading: The community and the king's peace
bullets: Most crimes were settled by the community
The king guaranteed peace across the land
Breaking the peace was an offence against the king
teach.note: Explain that in the 10th and 11th centuries there was no police force or prison system. Order depended on neighbours and local lords. Link to wergild, to be covered later.

practice: Give one example of a crime against the person, one against property and one against authority.
Name three factors that can cause change in crime and punishment.
Why did the king guarantee peace?
independent: Create a table of Anglo-Saxon crimes in three categories
Explain in 3 sentences how the Church might influence ideas about crime
Write a short paragraph: why did the community, not the state, have most responsibility for law and order c1000?
exit: What are the three categories of crime?
Which factor do you think changes punishment most? Explain.
lessons.homework: Read the lesson notes and make a one-page factor map listing six factors and one example of how each could change crime and punishment.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: crime categories table with examples to sort. Stretch: explain how a change in attitudes could change the definition of a crime.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Crime and punishment in medieval England, c1000-c1500
lessons.title: Anglo-Saxon law enforcement: tithings, hue and cry and courts
objectives: Describe how law and order was kept in Anglo-Saxon communities
Explain why the community had responsibility for catching criminals

keywords.def: a group of ten men responsible for each other's good behaviour
the duty to raise the alarm and chase a criminal
a local area made up of ten tithings, with its own court
the king's official who kept order in a shire; later called a sheriff
a landowner who gave protection and demanded service

starter: Name the three categories of crime.
Name two factors that cause change in crime and punishment.

teach.heading: A community responsibility
bullets: There was no police force
People policed themselves
Everyone was part of a community group
teach.note: Make the contrast with today's police, courts and prisons. Ask pupils: what are the advantages and disadvantages of a system in which neighbours police each other?

teach.heading: Tithings and the hundred
bullets: Every man over 12 joined a tithing of ten
If one broke the law the others had to bring him to court
Ten tithings made a hundred
teach.note: Misconception: tithings were run by officials. They were groups of neighbours; the tithing leader was the 'chief tithingman'. If a member fled, the group could be fined.

teach.heading: Hue and cry
bullets: Anyone who saw a crime had to shout
All villagers had to join the chase
People who ignored the cry could be fined
teach.note: Run a quick role-play: one pupil shouts 'Stop thief!', others respond. Ask why this worked best in small villages where everyone knew everyone.

teach.heading: Courts and the shire reeve
bullets: Hundred courts judged minor cases monthly
Shire courts handled serious matters, meeting twice a year
The shire reeve represented the king
teach.note: The shire reeve (the origin of 'sheriff') presided over the shire court with the bishop. Ask which court would hear a murder. Serious crime went to the king's officers; the system was local, not national.

practice: What was a tithing and what responsibility did it carry?
Describe how the hue and cry worked.
Which official kept order in the shire?
independent: Draw a diagram of the Anglo-Saxon system: individuals, tithing, hundred, shire
Write an answer to: Explain two ways in which Anglo-Saxon communities enforced the law
Evaluate: how effective was the community system? Give two strengths and two weaknesses
exit: Why was the hue and cry effective in villages?
lessons.homework: Write a 12-mark style paragraph: explain why community responsibility was important in Anglo-Saxon law enforcement.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: system diagram with labels to match. Stretch: compare Anglo-Saxon community policing with a modern neighbourhood watch.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Crime and punishment in medieval England, c1000-c1500
lessons.title: Anglo-Saxon trials and punishments: wergild, ordeal and oath-helpers
objectives: Describe Anglo-Saxon methods of trial and punishment
Explain why punishments were based on compensation and community

keywords.def: a fixed payment to a victim's family depending on the victim's status
a trial where God was believed to show guilt or innocence
a trial using oath-helpers who swore the accused was innocent
a person outside the protection of the law
a punishment that damages the body, such as cutting off a hand

starter: Who judged serious cases in the shire court?

teach.heading: Wergild and compensation
bullets: Wergild was 'man-price'
A killer paid the victim's family
The amount depended on the victim's rank
teach.note: Explain that this prevented blood feuds. An earl's life cost more than a peasant's. Ask pupils whether this is fair, and compare with modern ideas of equality before the law. In Islamic law, diyya is compensation; avoid equating the systems directly.

teach.heading: Trial by oath: compurgation
bullets: The accused swore an oath of innocence
Oath-helpers swore they believed him
More helpers were needed for serious charges
teach.note: Oath-helpers were of good character. Ask why this worked in tight-knit communities. A person's reputation was key evidence.

teach.heading: Trial by ordeal
bullets: Used when oaths were not enough or the accused had a bad reputation
Hot iron, hot water or cold water
Priests supervised; God was thought to judge
teach.note: Hot iron: carry iron three paces, bandage the hand; if healed after 3 days, innocent. Cold water: sink = innocent, float = guilty. Link to belief in God's intervention. Stress it was a religious process, not just cruelty.

teach.heading: Punishments
bullets: Fines and compensation for most crimes
Mutilation or death for serious crimes
Outlawry: anyone could kill an outlaw
teach.note: Use short examples. Ask: why was imprisonment rare? There were few prisons and the cost of keeping people was too high; punishments were quick and public.

practice: What was wergild and why was it used?
Explain how compurgation worked.
Why did people believe ordeals revealed the truth?
independent: Make a table: type of trial, how it worked, why it was used
Explain two ways in which Anglo-Saxon trials show the influence of religion
Write an answer: why did Anglo-Saxon punishment focus on compensation?
lessons.homework: Prepare a 12-mark answer: explain why trial by ordeal was used in Anglo-Saxon England.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: trial types match-up cards. Stretch: evaluate whether wergild was more fair or unfair than modern fines.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Crime and punishment in medieval England, c1000-c1500
lessons.title: Norman changes: Forest Laws, murdrum and control
objectives: Describe changes to law and order after the Norman Conquest
Assess the extent of continuity and change in 1066-1100

keywords.def: laws protecting royal hunting land and the king's deer
illegally hunting animals on someone else's land
a fine on a community if a Norman was found killed and the killer unknown
a fight between accuser and accused, believed to show who was right
something that stays the same over time

starter: What was the role of the Church in trials?

teach.heading: William's problem
bullets: Normans were a small ruling minority
They feared English rebellions
William wanted control and income
teach.note: Link to Y7 knowledge: castles, Domesday Book and the Harrying of the North. Ask: how would a new ruler stay safe if he is a foreigner?

teach.heading: Keeping Anglo-Saxon systems
bullets: Hue and cry continued
Shire and hundred courts continued
Sheriffs replaced shire reeves
teach.note: Stress continuity: William kept the Anglo-Saxon system because it worked and it served him. Many lords and sheriffs, though, were now Norman.

teach.heading: Forest Laws
bullets: Large areas were declared royal forest
Hunting deer or cutting wood became poaching
Punishments included blinding, mutilation or fines
teach.note: The most hated Norman change. The New Forest is the best-known. Ask why the king cared: hunting was a sport and a source of meat and money. Poaching was a new crime against the king's authority.

teach.heading: Murdrum and trial by combat
bullets: If a Norman was killed, the hundred paid 46 marks unless the killer was named
Trial by combat was introduced for Normans
Wergild declined; death penalty was used more
teach.note: The murdrum fine was a harsh collective punishment to protect Normans. Be careful with the claim that William ended capital punishment: sources say he preferred mutilation to death, but this is debated.

practice: Why did William keep the Anglo-Saxon system?
What were the Forest Laws?
Why was the murdrum fine introduced?
independent: Complete a continuity/change table for 1066-1100
Write an answer: Explain two ways in which Norman law enforcement was different from Anglo-Saxon
Answer: How far did the Norman Conquest change crime and punishment? (paragraph)
exit: Name one continuity and one change after 1066.
Who benefited from the Forest Laws?
lessons.homework: Write a PEEL paragraph: The Norman Conquest changed crime and punishment more than it kept things the same. Do you agree?
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: continuity and change sort cards. Stretch: compare William's methods with those of another ruler you have studied.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Crime and punishment in medieval England, c1000-c1500
lessons.title: Medieval law enforcement: sheriffs, constables and juries
objectives: Describe how law enforcement developed between 1100 and 1400
Explain why trial by jury replaced trial by ordeal

keywords.def: a local official chosen to keep order in a village or town
a group of local people who decide whether the accused is guilty
a local gentleman appointed to try less serious crimes, from 1361
a royal law or court session set up by the king
an official who investigates sudden or suspicious deaths, from 1194

starter: Why did William keep the Anglo-Saxon courts?

teach.heading: Royal government grows
bullets: Henry II strengthened royal justice in the 1160s-70s
Royal judges toured the country
Law became more common across England
teach.note: Henry II (1154-89) created travelling royal judges and the Assize of Clarendon (1166). Ask: why would a king want standard law? Money, control and order.

teach.heading: Juries of presentment
bullets: The Assize of Clarendon (1166) set up juries
Local men reported suspected criminals
They were not yet deciding guilt
teach.note: Distinguish this jury (accusing) from the modern trial jury (deciding). The change is gradual. Ask: why use local men? They knew the people involved.

teach.heading: The end of ordeal
bullets: In 1215 the Church banned priests from ordeals
Without priests, ordeals could not run
Trial by jury grew to replace them
teach.note: Fourth Lateran Council, 1215. This shows how the Church could cause change. England had a system in which juries decided guilt by the mid-13th century. Sometimes jurors were threatened or pressured.

teach.heading: Local officers
bullets: Constables and watchmen patrolled towns
Coroners investigated deaths from 1194
Justices of the Peace began in 1361
teach.note: Introduce the roles. JPs were local gentry: they could hear minor cases, arrest and punish. Ask pupils how this system links to a growing central government.

practice: What did the Assize of Clarendon do?
Why did trial by ordeal end?
What was the job of a coroner?
independent: Create a timeline from 1066 to 1361 showing changes in law enforcement
Write: Explain why trial by jury replaced trial by ordeal (12-mark style)
Rate the importance of three causes of change: Church, government, attitudes
exit: In which year did the Church ban priests from ordeals?
lessons.homework: Finish the 12-mark explanation on the end of trial by ordeal.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: timeline cards with dates and events. Stretch: assess which factor (Church or government) was more important in changing law enforcement.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Crime and punishment in medieval England, c1000-c1500
lessons.title: The Church and the law: sanctuary, benefit of clergy and heresy
objectives: Explain how the medieval Church influenced crime and punishment
Describe the changing definition of heresy

keywords.def: the right of clergy to be tried in Church courts with lighter punishments
protection from arrest inside a church for up to 40 days
believing something the Church says is wrong
followers of John Wycliffe who criticised the Church
a court that tried clergy and moral offences

starter: What is a jury of presentment?

teach.heading: A powerful Church
bullets: Almost everyone was Christian
The Church ran its own courts
It judged clergy and moral offences
teach.note: Be respectful but factual about the medieval Christian context; treat religions fairly. The Church also affected laws on marriage, wills and blasphemy.

teach.heading: Benefit of clergy
bullets: Priests could be tried in Church courts
Punishments were milder than in royal courts
Later, anyone who could read could claim it
teach.note: The 'neck verse' was Psalm 51 (read aloud). Ask: was this fair? Show how it could protect criminals who were not clergy. The system was gradually widened.

teach.heading: Sanctuary
bullets: Fugitives could shelter in a church
They had 40 days to confess or negotiate
Many then agreed to abjure the realm
teach.note: Abjuring meant swearing to leave the country by a set route. Sanctuary protected people from revenge killing but was sometimes abused.

teach.heading: Heresy and the Lollards
bullets: Wycliffe in the 1370s criticised Church wealth
Lollards wanted the Bible in English
In 1401 a law allowed burning of heretics
teach.note: De heretico comburendo, 1401. William Sawtre was the first heretic burned. Heresy was a crime against God and the state: a good example of changing definitions of crime. Link to the idea that religious beliefs affect law.

practice: What was benefit of clergy?
How did sanctuary work?
Why was heresy treated as a serious crime?
independent: Make a spider diagram of the Church's influence on law
Write an answer: Explain two ways in which the Church influenced medieval punishment
Judge: was the Church a force for fairness or for control? Support with evidence
lessons.homework: Prepare to compare how heresy and treason were treated: write a short table.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: matching cards for key terms. Stretch: evaluate whether the Church's influence increased or decreased between 1000 and 1400.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Crime and punishment in medieval England, c1000-c1500
lessons.title: Medieval punishment, the Black Death and new crimes
objectives: Describe medieval punishments and the reasons for them
Explain how the Black Death changed crime and the law

keywords.def: punishment inflicted on the body, such as whipping
the death penalty
the 1351 law fixing wages at pre-plague levels
a punishment meant to put people off committing crimes
the 1381 uprising against taxes and labour laws

starter: Name one Church influence on punishment.

teach.heading: Aims of punishment
bullets: Deterrence: put others off
Retribution: payback for the crime
Public shame: stocks and pillory
teach.note: Ask pupils to identify the aims in each example. Public punishments were seen as an effective deterrent, especially with no police to catch most criminals.

teach.heading: Types of punishment
bullets: Hanging for serious theft and murder
Whipping, stocks and pillory for minor crimes
Fines for selling short measures
teach.note: Theft of goods worth more than 12 pence could be a hanging offence. The Assize of Bread and Ale (1266) set rules for bakers and brewers. Bakers selling underweight loaves could be pulled through the streets on a hurdle.

teach.heading: The Black Death, 1348-49
bullets: Killed perhaps a third to a half of the population
Workers became scarce so wages rose
Landowners wanted to keep wages low
teach.note: Be clear that this was a plague which struck Britain in 1348. Ask how a labour shortage changes the balance of power between lord and peasant.

teach.heading: New crimes and revolt
bullets: The Statute of Labourers (1351) fixed wages
Breaking it became a crime
Anger over this and the poll tax led to the Peasants' Revolt (1381)
teach.note: Link to the Church and Crown: the Revolt was put down with force; leaders such as Wat Tyler were killed. Ask: why do laws sometimes create new criminals?

practice: Name two medieval punishments and their aims.
Why did the Black Death change wages?
What did the Statute of Labourers do?
independent: Make a table: crime, punishment, aim of punishment
Write: Explain why the Black Death led to new crimes
Answer: How far was deterrence the main aim of medieval punishment?
exit: Give one reason for the Statute of Labourers.
lessons.homework: Write a PEEL paragraph explaining one way the Black Death affected crime.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: crime-punishment-aim sorting cards. Stretch: evaluate the claim that medieval punishments were mainly about fear.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: Crime and punishment in medieval England, c1000-c1500
lessons.title: Review: continuity and change c1000-c1500 and exam practice
objectives: Summarise the main continuities and changes in crime, law enforcement and punishment c1000-c1500
Practise Edexcel thematic exam skills: explain why, similarity and judgement questions

keywords.def: a way two things are alike
a way two things are not alike
Point, Evidence, Explain, Link: a paragraph structure
an event or development that caused significant change
a reasoned conclusion about 'how far' something is true

starter: Give three Anglo-Saxon law enforcement features.
Give two changes the Normans made.

teach.heading: The big picture
bullets: Continuity: community responsibility, harsh punishment
Change: Norman Forest Laws, juries, JPs
The Church and the Crown drove most change
teach.note: Build a class timeline of c1000-c1500 on screen. Ask pupils to place 1066, 1166, 1215, 1351, 1361, 1401. Check they can explain why each date matters.

teach.heading: Explaining why
bullets: Use factors: Church, government, attitudes
Include specific evidence and dates
Link each point back to the question
teach.note: Model a 12-mark 'Explain why' paragraph: Point (trial by ordeal ended), Evidence (1215 Lateran Council), Explain (without priests it could not continue), Link (shows the Church as a cause of change).

teach.heading: Similarity and difference
bullets: Pick two specific points
Support each with precise knowledge
Explain why they are similar or different
teach.note: Example: hue and cry in Anglo-Saxon and Norman England; both relied on the community. Emphasise specific knowledge, not general statements.

teach.heading: How far do you agree?
bullets: Give both sides with evidence
Weigh the importance of each
End with a clear judgement
teach.note: Model on the statement: 'The Normans changed law and order more than the Church did between 1000 and 1400.' Show a plan with two reasons for, two against, and a conclusion that weighs them.

practice: State two similarities between Anglo-Saxon and Norman law enforcement.
Give two turning points and explain each in one sentence.
Plan a judgement answer in bullet points.
independent: Write a 12-mark answer: Explain why the Church was important in medieval law and order
Write a 16-mark style answer: 'The Norman Conquest was the most important turning point in c1000-c1500.' How far do you agree?
Self-assess using a mark scheme grid
exit: Name two factors that caused change c1000-c1500.
What makes a strong judgement paragraph?
lessons.homework: Complete a one-page revision sheet for Key Topic 1 with 10 key dates and 10 key terms.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: PEEL planning frame and word bank. Stretch: write a conclusion that ranks three turning points by importance.
